uncertainty_flags: Detection modules are limited to 'easy cases' (small lexica), so coverage of complex cases (scope, nested modals) is limited.
Preservation of intended meaning depends on annotation accuracy and whether annotations suffice to reconstruct clause-level semantics.

identified_claims.claim_text: Multiple minimization modes (MinIE-Safe, MinIE-Frequency, MinIE-Collocations, MinIE-Aggressive) allow a controllable trade-off between aggressiveness of minimization and precision/recall.
evidence: Sec. 6 describes four modes with differing rules and resources (e.g., dictionaries based on corpus frequency or collocations).
Empirical tables show different mean lengths and precision per mode (Table 3 & 4).
uncertainty_flags: Operational choices (frequency thresholds, dictionary sources) are heuristic and dataset-dependent; generality not shown.
Empirical evidence limited to NYT/Wiki; sensitivity across other domains not measured.

identified_claims.claim_text: MinIE produces much shorter (more minimal) extractions than ClausIE and many prior systems while achieving competitive or higher factual precision on evaluated datasets.
evidence: NYT-10k stats (Table 3): ClausIE mean length 10.9 vs MinIE modes 4.7–7.2; extraction counts reported.
Labeled samples (Table 4): MinIE-S factual precision ~0.79 (NYT) and ~0.83 (Wiki) higher than ClausIE and Stanford OIE in these samples.
uncertainty_flags: Labeled evaluations are small (n=200 each) and lack confidence intervals or inter-annotator agreement.
Comparability to baselines affected by CoreNLP versions and implementation choices; reported gains may be sensitive to toolchain.
Recall behavior varies; reductions in extractions may reflect de-duplication rather than loss of information—measurement depends on subsequence redundancy heuristic.

identified_claims.claim_text: Annotation of negative polarity and other factuality information addresses absence of negative evidence in prior OIE outputs and can improve downstream reasoning.
evidence: Paper claims to be first OIE to produce negative-polarity extractions; details in Sec. 5.1 on negation lexicon and annotation.
NYT-10k statistics report fractions of negative/potential annotations present in MinIE outputs.
uncertainty_flags: Negation detection lexicon tiny ({no, not, never, none}); complex negation scope and implicit negatives not handled.
No downstream task experiments to validate that annotations improve reasoning—claim is conceptual rather than empirically demonstrated.

identified_claims.claim_text: Some aggressive minimization modes reduce recall/number of extractions and can introduce errors due to parser/NER mistakes or missing collocations; errors are primarily caused by upstream NLP components and dictionary coverage.
evidence: Sec. 7.4 qualitative error analysis points to parsing and NER errors, and missing collocations in dictionary causing incorrect adjective drops.
Table 3/4 show fewer extractions in aggressive modes and precision drop in MinIE-A.
uncertainty_flags: Relative contribution of parser vs NER vs dictionary errors is not quantified—only qualitative examples provided.
Recall reduction measured with subsequence redundancy heuristic; can obscure whether information loss or redundancy reduction occurred.

strengths.title: Clear design separating surface facts from factuality markers
strengths.description: The paper explicitly separates minimal surface triples from polarity, modality, attribution, and quantities via annotations, providing a principled representation that addresses a recognized OIE shortcoming.
evidence: Introduction, Sec. 3 and Sec. 5 describe the annotation schema and basic minimization process.
Table 1 illustrates removal of negation from relation and recording as negative polarity annotation.

strengths.title: Practical multi-mode controllability
strengths.description: MinIE implements several operational modes (Safe, Frequency, Collocations, Aggressive) enabling explicit trade-offs between minimality and safety, useful for downstream consumers with different risk tolerances.
evidence: Sec. 6 details the modes and their resource/heuristic differences.
Empirical tables show how length and precision vary by mode.

strengths.title: Concrete implementation and planned release
strengths.description: MinIE is implemented on top of ClausIE with described procedures and the authors intend to release code, datasets, and labelling guidelines, facilitating reproducibility and community use.
evidence: Sec. 3 states implementation on ClausIE; Sec. 7.1 notes code/datasets/guidelines will be made public and submitted to SoftConf.
Detailed algorithmic rules for enrichment, PSS enumeration, and minimization modes are provided.

strengths.title: Empirical evidence of compactness
strengths.description: Large-scale corpus statistics (NYT-10k) show substantial reduction in mean extraction length across MinIE modes versus ClausIE, supporting the minimality objective.
evidence: Table 3: ClausIE µ=10.9, MinIE modes µ between 4.7 and 7.2 on NYT-10k.

concerns.title: Limited factuality detection coverage
concerns.description: Negation and modality detection use very small lexica and simple patterns limited to 'easy cases', so many complex phenomena (scope, double negation, implicit modality) are likely missed or misannotated, undermining the claim that annotations preserve factuality broadly.
evidence: Sec. 5.1 lists negation lexicon {no, not, never, none} and explicitly says MinIE restricts to easy cases.
Sec. 5.2 admits modality lexicon is small and focuses on CT vs PS only.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Quantify factuality detection recall/precision on a targeted corpus of varied negation/modality/attribution cases; report error types and consider integrating scope resolution or richer lexical resources (or supervised classifiers) for these phenomena.

concerns.title: Small labeled evaluation and missing reliability statistics
concerns.description: Main factual/attribution precision claims rest on two small 200-sentence labeled samples without reported inter-annotator agreement or confidence intervals, limiting statistical confidence in reported gains versus baselines.
evidence: Sec. 7.1: datasets NYT and Wiki are 200-sentence samples each; labeling procedure described but no IAA or CI reported.
Prior reviewers noted small n and lack of statistical testing.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide inter-annotator agreement on a subset, report confidence intervals or statistical tests for precision differences, and expand labeled sets (or perform bootstrapped significance testing) to strengthen empirical claims.

concerns.title: Dictionary construction heuristics & domain sensitivity
concerns.description: Frequency thresholds and external collocation resource choices are heuristic and evaluated only on NYT (MinIE-F trained on NYT), raising questions about transferability and reproducibility of the Frequency/Collocations modes.
evidence: Sec. 6.2 uses frequency threshold example ≥10 and builds MinIE-F dictionary from NYT corpus; MinIE-C uses WordNet/Wiktionary in experiments.
Authors acknowledge dictionary coverage affects minimization (Sec. 7.4).
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Include ablation studies varying frequency thresholds, compare alternative collocation sources, and evaluate MinIE-F/C on out-of-training-domain corpora to measure robustness.

concerns.title: Upstream component sensitivity not quantified
concerns.description: The system depends heavily on dependency parsing and NER; while parsing/NER errors are mentioned qualitatively as main error sources, their quantitative impact on minimization/precision is not measured.
evidence: Sec. 7.4 gives qualitative examples of parse/NER errors producing wrong minimizations.
Assumptions A2 and A5 in shared analysis highlight parser/NER reliance.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Run controlled experiments using oracle/degraded NER and/or parsers (or alternative parsers/NER models) to quantify error propagation; report how much precision/recall changes under these conditions.

concerns.title: Downstream utility of annotations untested
concerns.description: The claim that annotations (negation, modality, attribution, quantities) improve downstream reasoning is plausible but unsupported by experiments on downstream tasks.
evidence: Introduction and Sec. 8 argue conceptual benefits; no downstream task evaluation provided.
Sec. 7 focuses on extraction-level precision/length; no task-level validation.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Demonstrate the practical benefit via a downstream task (e.g., question answering, knowledge-base population with polarity-aware evaluation, or simple inference tests comparing systems with and without annotations).

concerns.title: Redundancy measure may bias recall comparisons
concerns.description: The non-redundant extraction measure treats subsequence triples as redundant, a syntactic heuristic that may not reflect semantic redundancy and can advantage systems producing more minimal triples.
evidence: Sec. 7.1 explicitly defines redundancy as subsequence membership within same-sentence outputs.
Shared analysis notes this heuristic's limitations.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Complement the subsequence heuristic with semantic clustering or human judgment on redundancy for a subset, and report sensitivity of non-redundant counts to the redundancy definition.

comparable_works.relevance: Introduced frequency-based lexical constraint to avoid overly-specific relations; conceptual precursor to MinIE-F.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Similarity: frequency heuristic to judge relation stability. Difference: MinIE generalizes frequency idea to subjects/arguments and integrates factuality annotations.
comparable_works.source_trace: Paper references and Sec. 2 & 6.2

comparable_works.relevance: An aggressive minimization OIE system against which MinIE compares; shares goal of minimizing surface material.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Similarity: aggressive deletion of certain typed dependencies. Difference: MinIE separates factuality annotations and offers multi-mode dictionary-driven control; MinIE reports higher precision in some modes.
comparable_works.source_trace: Sec. 2 Related work

comparable_works.relevance: Introduced annotated OIE extractions (attribution and clause modifiers).
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Similarity: use of annotations for attribution/clause modifiers. Difference: MinIE extends annotations to polarity, modality, quantities and claims negative-polarity extraction novelty.
comparable_works.source_trace: Sec. 1 and Sec. 2

comparable_works.relevance: Base system on which MinIE is implemented; provides clause decomposition and input extractions.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Similarity: clause-based extraction backbone. Difference: MinIE builds enrichment, basic minimization, and multiple aggressive modes atop ClausIE.
comparable_works.source_trace: Sec. 3 and Sec. 4.1

comparable_works.relevance: Factuality representation (polarity/modality) inspired MinIE’s annotation schema.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Similarity: use of polarity and modality labels. Difference: MinIE implements a lightweight detection approach geared to OIE pipeline rather than a full factuality system.
comparable_works.source_trace: Sec. 5 references

uncertainty_flags: Factuality detectors limited to small lexica and 'easy cases' — scope and complex phenomena likely missed.
Labeled evaluation sets small (n=200 each) with no inter-annotator agreement or confidence intervals reported.
Dictionary and frequency thresholds are heuristic and trained on NYT (MinIE-F), so cross-domain robustness is uncertain.
Comparisons to baselines may be confounded by NLP toolchain (CoreNLP) versions and implementation differences.
Error attribution to parsing vs NER vs dictionary coverage is qualitative; no quantitative decomposition provided.
alternative_interpretations: Precision gains reported for conservative MinIE modes may partially come from removing difficult long/complex extractions (thus reducing the number of risky outputs), not solely from superior annotation/minimization logic.
Reduced extraction counts in aggressive modes could reflect both desired de-duplication and unwanted information loss; the subsequence redundancy heuristic may mask true recall loss.
MinIE’s advantage over certain baselines could be influenced by implementation/toolchain differences (e.g., CoreNLP version), not just algorithmic improvements.
transparency_notes: Code, datasets, and labelling guidelines are stated to be released; reproducing results requires the same NLP stack (CoreNLP 3.5.1) per authors' notes.

Paper provides algorithmic detail for enrichment and minimization modes, but many operational hyperparameters (e.g., exact frequency thresholds, lexicon sizes) should be explicitly listed in released artifacts for reproducibility.

Qualitative error analysis is useful but a quantitative breakdown of error sources (parsing vs NER vs dictionary mismatch) is absent; authors could provide reproduction scripts to enable community analysis.

creativity_safeguard.novelty_not_validity_note: The idea of annotating factuality markers while minimizing surface triples shows limited precedent (OLLIE for attribution), so the contribution is reasonably novel; novelty does not guarantee accuracy or broad applicability, which require further empirical validation (especially factuality coverage and downstream utility).
counterfactual_conditions_for_success: If richer factuality modules (scope-aware negation, learned modality classifiers) are integrated, MinIE-style annotations could reliably preserve factual meaning while yielding compact extractions.

If dictionaries for collocations are expanded (including domain-specific resources) and/or PSS matching improved, frequency/collocations modes would keep essential collocations and avoid erroneous adjective drops.
If downstream tasks are shown to benefit from annotated minimal triples (e.g., polarity-aware KB population or QA), then the approach will have practical impact despite current detection limits.

If controlled experiments show that parser/NER improvements (or oracle inputs) significantly increase precision, then MinIE’s design is validated as being mainly upstream-component-limited rather than conceptually flawed.

novelty_lenses.rationale: MinIE builds on established OIE systems and ideas (ClausIE, ReVerb frequency heuristic, OLLIE annotations) and contributes practical engineering: explicit factuality/quantity annotations plus multi-mode dictionary-driven minimization. This is a clear incremental but useful methodological advance.
evidence: Paper integrates enrichment, annotations for polarity/modality/quantities, and mode-based minimization.
Related work section situates MinIE relative to ReVerb, OLLIE, and Stanford OIE.
uncertainty_flags: Empirical validation scope limited; generalization and practical downstream benefits not yet established.

novelty_lenses.rationale: The conceptual move—decoupling minimal fact triples from factuality markers via structured annotations—could materially change how extracted facts are consumed for reasoning tasks. However, the current realization relies on simple detectors and limited evaluation; disruptive impact depends on improving factuality coverage and demonstrating downstream gains.
evidence: Annotations for negation/modality/quantities are rarely present in prior OIE outputs; authors highlight this gap.
Paper argues that lack of negative evidence is a concern for downstream reasoning and provides annotated output as a remedy.
uncertainty_flags: No downstream task experiments, limited detectors, and dataset-dependent dictionaries leave disruptive claims speculative.

confidence_interval.rationale: Confidence expresses the reviewer’s belief that the core engineering approach (minimization + annotations) is sound and the empirical results are indicative but not definitive. Lower bound reflects methodological concerns (small labeled sets, limited factuality detection, lack of statistical testing and downstream validation). Upper bound reflects clear evidence of extraction compactness on a large corpus and plausible precision improvements in conservative modes.

consensus_findings: MinIE is a coherent, implemented system built on ClausIE that (a) enriches relations, (b) removes polarity/modality/attribution/quantity markers from surface triples and records them as structured annotations, and (c) offers multiple minimization modes (Safe, Frequency, Collocations, Aggressive) to trade off minimality and safety.

Empirical evidence shows MinIE substantially reduces mean extraction length on a large NYT-10k extraction set versus ClausIE and other baselines; conservative minimization modes (Safe/Frequency/Collocations) tend to preserve or improve factual precision on the small labeled samples provided.

The paper explicitly acknowledges key limitations: factuality detection is lexicon- and pattern-limited to 'easy cases'; minimization decisions depend on heuristic dictionary construction (frequency thresholds and collocation resources); and many errors stem from upstream dependency parsing and NER.
Authors intend to release code, datasets, extraction outputs, and labelling guidelines, which supports reproducibility and further community validation.
disagreements: Extent of empirical support for precision claims: some reviewers emphasize the positive signal in the labeled samples (directionally convincing), while others stress that sample sizes (n=200) and lack of inter-annotator agreement or statistical tests limit the generality of precision claims.

Interpretation of novelty: several reviewers view MinIE as a valuable incremental engineering integration of prior ideas (ClausIE, ReVerb-style frequency heuristics, OLLIE annotations) while at least one reviewer frames the conceptual move (explicit separation of minimal surface facts from factuality/quantity annotations) as relatively novel and potentially disruptive. Both perspectives are supported by the manuscript but emphasize different novelty lenses.

Practical readiness: some reviewers judge the system design and modes as practically useful now (with caveats), whereas others require further validation (parser/NER sensitivity, dictionary ablations, downstream-task evidence) before endorsing real-world adoption.
uncertainty_hotspots: Factuality detection coverage: negation, modality and attribution modules rely on very small lexica and simple patterns; scope resolution, double negation, implicit modality and varied attribution constructions are not handled and may create systematic annotation failures.

Upstream-component sensitivity: the degree to which dependency parser and NER errors drive MinIE's precision/recall outcomes is not quantified; no oracle/degraded ablations were reported to isolate their contribution.

Dictionary and threshold choices: MinIE-F frequency thresholds and MinIE-C collocation resource coverage are heuristic and dataset-dependent; sensitivity of minimization decisions and cross-domain transfer are unmeasured.

Evaluation reliability: labeled precision/attribution results rest on two 200-sentence samples without reported inter-annotator agreement or confidence intervals; differences across systems/modes may not be statistically robust.
Redundancy and recall measurement: non-redundant extraction counts use a syntactic subsequence heuristic that can misrepresent semantic redundancy and thus bias recall/compactness comparisons.
model_diversity_effects: Structure-focused reviewers highlighted logical coherence, clear mapping from problem to design, and the value of mode-based control; this emphasizes strengths in engineering rationale and pipeline clarity.

Methodology/auditing reviewers foregrounded reproducibility, sensitivity analyses, and statistical reliability, flagging missing ablations and measurement rigor; this emphasizes evaluation and robustness gaps.

Novelty assessors diverged: incremental-lens reviewers see MinIE as an engineering synthesis of known techniques, while disruptive-lens reviewers treat the annotation-first minimality framing as a noteworthy conceptual contribution; this divergence affects perceived impact and future research directions.

Claim-verifier reviewers concentrated on evidence matching claims and produced conservative caveats around overstatements; combined with other roles, this produces a balanced view that the concept is promising but empirical validation is currently limited.
meta_review.editor_guidance: Frame editorial next steps around targeted validation rather than a single accept/reject judgement. Prioritize requests that increase empirical reliability and isolate mechanisms: (1) report inter-annotator agreement and statistical confidence intervals (or bootstrap estimates) for labeled precision/attribution numbers and clarify labelling guidelines; (2) provide ablation experiments isolating upstream error effects (oracle NER/parser or alternative parsers/NERs) and quantify how much parsing/NER errors affect minimization/precision; (3) present sensitivity analysis for dictionary construction (vary frequency thresholds, ablate WordNet/Wiktionary sources, and test domain transfer between NYT and Wiki); (4) include at least one lightweight downstream evaluation (e.g., polarity-aware KB filtering, QA filtering, or simple fact verification) to substantiate claims about annotation utility; (5) publish exact dictionaries, lexica and toolchain versions used to enable reproducibility. Maintain the editor’s role to weigh the importance of these additional experiments given venue constraints and to prioritize which experiments are mandatory vs. suggested for future work.
meta_review.author_guidance: To strengthen claims and address principal uncertainties, provide the following: (1) labeling reliability: publish labeling guidelines and inter-annotator agreement on a subset; report confidence intervals or statistical tests for precision differences; (2) upstream sensitivity: run oracle and alternative upstream-component ablations (oracle NER and/or dependency parses, or alternate parsers/NER models) and report how precision/recall shift; (3) dictionary/distance sensitivity: vary frequency thresholds, ablate collocation resources, and test MinIE-F trained on one domain and evaluated on another to show transfer behavior; (4) factuality coverage: quantify factuality annotation recall/precision on a curated challenge set (negation scope, double negation, nested modality, implicit attribution) and discuss integration paths for richer factuality modules; (5) redundancy metric robustness: complement subsequence heuristic with a semantic clustering or human-validated redundancy measure for a sample and report how conclusions change; (6) provide at least one downstream-task experiment demonstrating practical benefit of annotations or explicitly delimit claims as conceptual until such validation is available; (7) release exact dictionaries, lexica, CoreNLP/toolchain versions, and code as promised to enable replication and community-driven follow-up.
transparency_report: Authors state intent to release code, datasets, extractions, labels, and labelling guidelines, which is necessary to reproduce and extend results; publication of these artifacts is essential for verifying dictionary construction, lexica, and labelling rules.

The manuscript reports the CoreNLP version used and notes that baseline behaviors depend on toolchain versions; authors should publish exact preprocessing scripts and environment (or container) to eliminate replication ambiguity.

Key operational hyperparameters (exact frequency thresholds, the full collocation lists, negation/modality lexica) are described heuristically in-text but should be provided verbatim in the release to ensure reproducibility.

Evaluation protocol is described (entailment-based labeling with annotations taken into account) but lacks inter-annotator agreement and confidence intervals; the labeling guidelines must be released and IAA reported to interpret precision numbers.

Error analysis is qualitative and contains helpful examples, but authors should release error-coded examples and, if possible, a quantitative breakdown of error sources to support claims about upstream-component effects.
epistemic_limits: The reviewers’ synthesis rests on the manuscript's reported experiments and qualitative analyses; primary epistemic limitations are (a) small labeled-sample sizes for precision claims and missing inter-annotator agreement, which constrain generalization and statistical confidence; (b) absence of ablations isolating upstream parser/NER error contributions and dictionary sensitivity, leaving the causal source of many errors underdetermined; (c) lexicon- and pattern-limited factuality detection that systematically under-represents complex negation/modality phenomena, so claims about preserved factuality are bounded to 'easy cases'; and (d) lack of downstream-task validation, which means asserted benefits for reasoning and KB construction remain hypothetical. These gaps imply that while engineering and conceptual contributions are substantiated at an initial level, conclusions about generality, robustness, and downstream impact should be treated as provisional until the recommended additional experiments and artifact releases are made available.

human_facing_meta_review.summary: The manuscript presents MinIE, an implemented Open Information Extraction (OIE) pipeline built on ClausIE that (1) enriches relations, (2) removes polarity, modality, attribution and quantities from surface triples and records them as structured annotations, and (3) applies controllable minimization modes (Safe, Frequency, Collocations, Aggressive) to drop additional modifiers. Empirical evidence shows substantial reduction in mean extraction length on a large NYT-10k extraction set, and on two small labeled 200-sentence samples conservative MinIE modes report higher factual precision than several baselines. The design is coherent and practically oriented, but empirical claims have epistemic limits tied to small labeled sets, lexicon/pattern-limited factuality detection, heuristic dictionary construction, and unquantified upstream-component sensitivity.
strengths: Clear conceptual contribution: explicit separation of minimal surface triples from factuality/quantity/attribution annotations, operationalized in an implemented system.
Practical, mode-driven design offering explicit control over aggressiveness vs safety (Safe/Frequency/Collocations/Aggressive) that is useful for diverse application risk profiles.
Substantial corpus-scale evidence of compactness (NYT-10k mean extraction length reductions relative to ClausIE) and side-by-side comparisons with multiple OIE baselines.
Authors acknowledge major limitations, provide qualitative error analysis (parser/NER/dictionary), and commit to releasing code, datasets, and labeling guidelines to support reproducibility.
limitations: Factuality-detection coverage is limited: negation and modality detection rely on small lexica and simple patterns (authors admit focusing on 'easy cases'); scope, double negation, nested modality and many implicit forms are not handled, so annotations do not guarantee preservation of factual meaning beyond simple instances.

Evaluation reliability concerns: key factual-precision/attribution claims rest on two small labeled samples (n=200 each) without reported inter-annotator agreement or confidence intervals; statistical robustness and generalization are therefore uncertain.

Dictionary and hyperparameter heuristics under-specified: MinIE-F frequency thresholds and MinIE-C collocation resources are chosen heuristically and trained/assembled on NYT or WordNet/Wiktionary; sensitivity to threshold choice and cross-domain transfer are not quantified.

Upstream-component sensitivity not isolated: dependency parsing and NER are central to enrichment and minimization steps but no oracle/degraded ablations or quantitative breakdowns attribute how much error stems from parser vs NER vs dictionary coverage.
open_questions: Please provide inter-annotator agreement (IAA) on the labeled NYT/Wiki subsets and report confidence intervals or statistical tests for reported precision differences. If not available, can authors expand labeled sets or present bootstrap CI to support precision claims?

Can the authors quantify upstream error contributions? Specifically, please run oracle/degraded ablations (e.g., oracle NER, oracle dependency parses, or alternative parser/NER models) to measure how much precision/recall shifts when upstream components are perfect or varied.

How sensitive are MinIE-F/MinIE-C decisions to dictionary construction choices? Please report ablations varying frequency thresholds, and an experiment training D on NYT but testing on Wiki (and vice versa) to assess domain transfer.

What is the empirical precision/recall of the factuality annotations themselves (polarity/modality/attribution/quantity) on a curated challenge set that includes negation scope, double negation, nested modality, and varied attribution constructions? If not measured, can authors supply such an evaluation or clarify limits of downstream claims?
consensus_snapshot: Reviewers agree MinIE is a coherent system that meaningfully reduces surface extraction length and that the annotation-first design (polarity/modality/attribution/quantity as metadata) is a valuable representational idea.
Conservative minimization modes (Safe/Frequency/Collocations) show a positive empirical signal on small labeled samples, while aggressive minimization trades precision for compactness.

Key limitations (limited factuality lexica, heuristic dictionaries, parser/NER dependence, small labeled evaluations) are acknowledged by authors and identified by reviewers as principal threats to claim generality.
disagreement_snapshot: Degree of novelty: some reviewers view MinIE as a useful incremental engineering integration of prior ideas (ClausIE, ReVerb frequency heuristics, OLLIE annotations), while others treat the explicit minimal-triple-plus-annotation framing as comparatively novel and conceptually impactful.

Interpretation of precision improvements: several reviewers consider the labeled-sample precision gains directionally persuasive, whereas others emphasize that small sample size and lack of statistical measures make the gains inconclusive without additional validation.
Practical readiness: reviewers diverge on whether MinIE is production-ready (with caveats) versus promising but requiring further robustness and downstream validation before practical adoption.
uncertainty_snapshot: Uncertainty about factuality annotation recall and precision beyond 'easy cases' due to small lexica and lack of scope-aware detection.
Uncertainty about how much parsing and NER errors drive end-to-end precision; absent ablations, causal attribution is underdetermined.
Uncertainty about minimization mode generality because dictionary thresholds and collocation lists are heuristic and possibly domain-specific.
Uncertainty about downstream utility: annotations are plausible aids for reasoning/KB tasks but no downstream experiments were provided to substantiate this.
source_trace: ClausIE implementation and clause-based extraction as MinIE backbone: Del Corro & Gemulla (2013) — referenced in paper Sec.3 and used as base system.
Frequency-based lexical constraint inspiration (ReVerb): Fader et al. (2011) — cited in Sec.6.2 as rationale for frequency thresholding.
Annotated OIE precedent (attribution/clausal modifiers): Schmitz et al. (OLLIE, 2012) — compared in Sec.2 and Sec.5 as conceptual predecessor for annotations.
Factuality representation foundation: Saurí & Pustejovsky (2012) — informs CT/PS polarity/modality labels; authors explicitly reference this in Sec.5 and adapt a simplified lexicon.

Toolchain sensitivity note: CoreNLP versioning (authors used CoreNLP 3.5.1) affecting baselines and parsing outputs — mentioned in Sec.7 and shared analyses; reproducing results requires matching toolchain versions.
transparency_notes: Manuscript provides algorithmic detail and states intent to release code, datasets, extractions, labels, and labeling guidelines. However, at present exact operational artifacts that matter for reproducibility (complete dictionaries/lexica, exact frequency thresholds, code for redundancy/non-redundant counting, and labeling guidelines and IAA) must be published. The authors report the CoreNLP version used; releasing containerized environments or scripts would further reduce replication ambiguity. Error-annotated examples and any ablation scripts would materially increase transparency.
human_facing_meta_review.editor_guidance: Prioritize requests that increase empirical reliability and isolate mechanisms behind claimed gains. Essential follow-ups: (1) Require reporting of inter-annotator agreement on labeled samples and confidence intervals (or bootstrap CI) for precision estimates; (2) Request upstream sensitivity ablations (oracle/degraded NER and/or parses or alternative parser/NER runs) to quantify error propagation; (3) Ask for dictionary-sensitivity experiments (vary frequency thresholds, ablate collocation sources) and a simple domain-transfer test (train D on NYT, test on Wiki or vice versa). Strongly encourage at least one lightweight downstream-task experiment (e.g., polarity-aware KB filtering or a small fact-verification probe) to substantiate applied claims. If venue constraints prevent additional experiments, require that authors explicitly limit claims about generality and downstream benefits and commit to releasing all artifacts (dictionaries, lexica, code, labeling guidelines, and scripts) on publication.
human_facing_meta_review.author_guidance: To strengthen empirical claims and reduce key uncertainties, provide: (1) labeling reliability: publish labeling guidelines and inter-annotator agreement on a subset; report confidence intervals or statistical tests for precision differences; (2) upstream-component ablations: run experiments with oracle NER and/or parses or with alternative parsers/NER models and report effect on precision/recall; (3) dictionary sensitivity: vary frequency thresholds, ablate WordNet/Wiktionary sources, and test MinIE-F/C transfer across NYT/Wiki to show robustness; (4) factuality annotation evaluation: assess precision/recall of polarity/modality/attribution/quantity detection on a curated challenge set including negation scope, double negation, nested modality, and implicit attribution; (5) redundancy/recall robustness: complement subsequence heuristic with a semantic clustering or human-validated redundancy check on a sample; (6) at least one downstream validation (small-scale task showing annotations help or a careful statement delimiting applied claims if not feasible); and (7) release exact dictionaries, lexica, toolchain versions, scripts and code (or container) as promised to enable reproduction and community evaluation.
human_facing_meta_review.comments:
Summary:
MinIE is an implemented OIE pipeline built on ClausIE that (a) pushes informative constituents into relation phrases, (b) performs basic minimization by removing polarity, modality, attribution and quantities from surface triples and recording them as structured annotations, and (c) applies multiple minimization modes (Safe, Frequency, Collocations, Aggressive) to control aggressiveness. Empirical evidence shows large reductions in mean extraction length on NYT-10k and a positive precision signal for conservative modes on two small labeled samples.

Strengths:
- Clear conceptual separation between minimal surface triple and factuality/quantity/attribution annotations, operationalized in code.
- Mode-based design affords practical control over aggressiveness vs safety for downstream users.
- Corpus-scale evidence of compactness and comparative evaluation to established OIE baselines.
- Authors acknowledge limitations, provide qualitative error analysis, and commit to releasing artifacts for reproducibility.

Limitations:
- Factuality modules are lexicon- and pattern-limited ('easy cases' only); scope and complex negation/modality constructs are not handled, so annotation coverage and correctness beyond simple forms are uncertain.
- Labeled evaluations are small (n=200 each) and lack reported inter-annotator agreement and statistical confidence intervals, weakening the statistical support for precision claims.
- Dictionary construction (frequency thresholds, collocation lists) is heuristic and dataset-dependent; sensitivity and cross-domain transfer are unquantified.
- Dependence on dependency parsing and NER is central but no oracle/degraded ablations or quantitative error attribution were performed to isolate their impact on precision.

Open Questions:
- What are inter-annotator agreement scores for the entailment/attribution labeling protocol, and what are confidence intervals (or bootstrap estimates) for the reported precision values? If unavailable, please provide them or expand labeling to enable reliable statistics.
- How much of MinIE's error budget is caused by dependency parsing vs NER vs dictionary misses? Please run oracle/degraded ablations (oracle NER or parses or alternative parser/NER) and report precision/recall shifts to attribute error sources quantitatively.
- How sensitive are MinIE-F and MinIE-C to dictionary construction choices (frequency thresholds, collocation sources)? Please provide ablations varying thresholds and an experiment testing domain transfer (train dictionary on NYT, test on Wiki and vice versa).
- What is the precision/recall of factuality annotations (polarity/modality/attribution/quantity) on a targeted challenge set including negation scope, double negation, nested modality, and implicit attribution? If not evaluated, can authors provide such an assessment or clearly qualify downstream-utility claims?

Transparency:
Authors provide algorithmic details and state intent to release code, datasets, extractions, labels and labeling guidelines. To enable reproduction and independent validation, the release must include exact dictionaries/lexica, frequency thresholds, scripts for redundancy/non-redundant counting, environment/toolchain versions (CoreNLP 3.5.1 was used), labeling guidelines and the labeled data (including adjudication notes), and error-coded examples. Containerized environments or scripts to recreate the exact preprocessing would further improve reproducibility.

confidence_interval.rationale: Lower bound reflects concerns about small labeled evaluations, limited factuality detection, heuristic dictionaries, and lack of ablation isolating upstream error contributions. Upper bound reflects consistent engineering design, clear conceptual framing (minimal triple + annotations), large-corpus evidence for compactness (NYT-10k), and positive directional results on labeled samples—conditional on addressing the methodological gaps noted above.

Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: 1. Skim-reading: adjusting your expectations.
Codes: none
Applies To: claim_verifier, meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, novelty_disruptive, novelty_incremental, structure_analyst
Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Hindsight bias may make things seem obvious in retrospect, and confirmation bias may make you dismiss evidence that contradicts your beliefs. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.
